{{short description|Theorem in general relativity}}
[[File:Central pressure evolution of uniform density star.png|thumb|right|300px|Evolution of central pressure against compactness (radius over mass) for a uniform density 'star'. This central pressure diverges at the Buchdahl bound.]]

In [[general relativity]], '''Buchdahl's theorem''', named after [[Hans Adolf Buchdahl]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Buchdahl |first1= H.A. |date=15 November 1959 |title=General relativistic fluid spheres|journal=Physical Review |volume=116 |issue=4 |pages=1027–1034 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.116.1027}}</ref> makes more precise the notion that there is a maximal sustainable density for ordinary gravitating matter. It gives an inequality between the mass and radius that must be satisfied for static, spherically symmetric matter configurations under certain conditions. In particular, for an areal radius <math>R</math>, the mass <math>M</math> must satisfy

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math> M < \frac{4 R c^2}{9G} </math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #ffffff
|background colour = #ffffff}}

where  <math> G </math> is the [[gravitational constant]] and  <math>c</math> is the [[speed of light]]. (An areal radius <math> R </math> corresponds to a sphere of surface area <math> 4 \pi R^2 </math>. In curved spacetime the proper radius of such a sphere is not necessarily <math> R </math>.)  This inequality is often referred to as '''Buchdahl's bound'''. The bound has historically also been called Schwarzschild's limit as it was first noted by [[Karl Schwarzschild]] to exist in the special case of a constant density fluid.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Grøn |first1= Øyvind |date=2016|title=Celebrating the centenary of the Schwarzschild solutions|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=84 |issue=537 |doi=10.1119/1.4944031|hdl=10642/4278|hdl-access=free}}</ref> However, this terminology should not be confused with the [[Schwarzschild radius]] which is notably smaller than the radius at the Buchdahl bound.

== Theorem ==
Given a static, spherically symmetric solution to the [[Einstein equations]] (without [[cosmological constant]]) with matter confined to an areal radius <math> R </math> that behaves as a [[perfect fluid]] with a [[density]] that does not increase outwards. Assume, in addition, that the density and pressure cannot be negative. The mass of this solution must satisfy

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math> M < \frac{4 R c^2}{9G} </math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #ffffff
|background colour = #ffffff}}

For his proof of the theorem, Buchdahl uses the [[TOV equation|Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equation]].

== Significance ==
The Buchdahl theorem is useful when looking for alternatives to [[black holes]]. Such attempts are often inspired by the [[Black hole information paradox|information paradox]]; a way to explain (part of) the [[dark matter]]; or to criticize that observations of black holes are based on excluding known astrophysical alternatives (such as [[neutron stars]]) rather than direct evidence. However, to provide a viable alternative it is sometimes needed that the object should be extremely compact and in particular violate the Buchdahl inequality. This implies that one of the assumptions of Buchdahl's theorem must be invalid. A classification scheme can be made based on which assumptions are violated.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cardoso |first1= Vitor|last2=Pani |first2=Paolo|date=2019|title=Testing the nature of dark compact objects: a status report|journal=Living Reviews in Relativity|volume=22 |issue=1 |doi=10.1007/s41114-019-0020-4 |arxiv=1904.05363|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Special Cases ==
=== Incompressible fluid ===
The special case of the incompressible fluid or constant density, <math> \rho(r) = \rho_* </math> for <math> r < R </math>, is a historically important example as, in 1916, Schwarzschild noted for the first time that the mass could not exceed the value <math> \frac{4 R c^2}{9G} </math> for a given radius <math> R </math> or the central pressure would become infinite. It is also a particularly tractable example. Within the star one finds,<ref>{{cite book |author=Carroll |first=Sean M. |author-link=Sean M. Carroll |title=Spacetime and Geometry: An Introduction to General Relativity |title-link=Spacetime and Geometry |date= |publisher=Addison-Wesley |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-8053-8732-2 |location=San Francisco}}</ref>

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math> m(r) = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho_* </math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #ffffff
|background colour = #ffffff}}

and using the TOV-equation

{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math> p(r) = \rho_* c^2 \frac{R \sqrt{R-2GM/c^2}-\sqrt{R^3-2GMr^2/c^2}}{\sqrt{R^3-2GMr^2/c^2}-3R\sqrt{R-2GM/c^2}}  </math>
|cellpadding
|border
|border colour = #ffffff
|background colour = #ffffff}}

such that the central pressure, <math> p(0) </math>, diverges as <math> R \to 9GM/4c^2 </math>.

== Extensions ==
Extensions to Buchdahl's theorem generally either relax assumptions on the matter or on the symmetry of the problem. For instance, by introducing anisotropic matter <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ivanov |first1= Boiko|date=2002 |title=Maximum bounds on the surface redshift of anisotropic stars|journal=Physical Review D|volume=65 |issue=10 |page=14011 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.65.104011|arxiv=gr-qc/0201090 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Barraco |first1= Daniel|last2=Hamity |first2= Victor|last3=Gleiser |first3=Reinaldo |date=2003 |title=Anisotropic spheres in general relativity reexamined|journal=Physical Review D|volume=67 |issue=6 |article-number=064003 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.67.064003}}</ref> or rotation.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Klenk |first1= Jürgen|date=1998 |title=Geometric properties of rotating stars in general relativity|journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity|volume=15 |issue=10 |page=3203 |doi=10.1088/0264-9381/15/10/021}}</ref> In addition one can also consider analogues of Buchdahl's theorem in other theories of gravity <ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rituparno |first1= Goswami|last2=Maharaj |first2= Sunil|last3=Nzioki |first3=Anne Marie |date=2015 |title=Buchdahl-Bondi limit in modified gravity: packing extra effective mass in relativistic compact stars|journal=Physical Review D|volume=92 |issue=6 |article-number=064002 |doi=10.1103/10.1103/PhysRevD.92.064002}}</ref><ref>
{{cite journal|first1=W.-X. |last1=Feng|first2=C.-Q. |last2=Geng|first3=L.-W. |last3=Luo |date=2019 |title=The Buchdahl stability bound in Eddington-inspired Born-Infeld gravity |journal=Chinese Physics C |volume=43 |issue=8 |article-number=083107 |doi=10.1088/1674-1137/43/8/083107|arxiv=1810.06753 }}</ref>
